newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: AUSTRALIAN BROADCASTING CORP MORNING UPDATE.
newsitem.headline: AUSTRALIAN BROADCASTING CORP MORNING UPDATE.

text.p: ARL PONDERS COMPROMISE WITH SUPER LEAGUE
The Board of the Australian Rugby League and club chief executives will meet today to consider a league compromise proposal that could see one competition next year.
Super League wants financial control of rugby league while the ARL still has a eye for running it.
The ARL Board, New South Wales Rugby League Board and club chief executives will hold separate meetings.
While it appears there may be some progress on who will spend the money and run the game, the big sticking point is still which teams will be part of a united competition and how fans will react.
ARL Chief Executive Neil Whittaker said that is an issue still to be addressed, but he is optimistic a compromise can be achieved.
But the make-up of teams for the competition is already causing headaches.
Perth Reds Chairman Stephen Edwards said some Sydney clubs are working to keep Perth out of a national competition.
Super League will watch results of the ARL meetings with interest, hoping for a positive reaction to the plan for a united league next year.
Super League clubs' executives gave in-principle support to the compromise plan.
THOUSANDS OF BOOKS DAMAGED IN UNIVERSITY LIBRARY FIRE
Up to 100,000 books have been damaged or destroyed in a library fire at Deakin University causing damage estimated at up to $2 million.
High powered fans were used to blow away thick smoke as crews battled to control the fire at the university's Rusden campus at Clayton in Melbourne's eastern suburbs.
Fire services controller Trevor Woodward said the flames were fuelled by more 11,000 newly delivered books.
He said 40 fire fighters fought the blaze which took hold in a store room in the building.
Australians qualify for two finals in Athens
Australia's Melinda Gainsford-Taylor has qualified for tomorrow's final of the 200 metres at the World Athletics Championships in Athens.
Gainsford-Taylor came fourth in her semi-final and was slowest to qualify in 22.70 seconds, but will line up for her first World Championships final.
American Inger Miller won the heat in 22 point 59 seconds and Jamaican star and defending champion Merlene Ottey won the other semi-final in 22 point 25 seconds.
Olympic champion Marie-Jose Perec was a late scratching from the semi-final after straining a hamstring muscle in the warm up.
Australian five thousand metres champion Kate Anderson came ninth in her 5,000 metres heat to qualify last for Saturday's final.
Australian Discus thrower Lisa-Marie Vizaniari finished last in the womens' discus final, throwing 55 point 20 and 57 point 56 metres.
New Zealand's Beatrice Faumuina won the gold medal with a throw of 66 point 82 two metres.
Ellina Zvereva of Belarus took silver, with Russian Natalia Sadova picking up bronze.
PET'S BASKET TOO HOT FOR COMFORT
Keeping the household pet warm on winter nights proved a costly exercise in the small town of Templers north of Adelaide last night.
A fire started in an electric blanket in a pet's basket caused $15,000 dollars damage to a home unit.
The Counrty Fire Service says the owner apparently went out leaving the pet's blanket turned on and there was an electrical fault.
A spokesperson says the pet wasn't in the basket at the time of the fire.
TEMPORARY BREAKTHROUGH IN MELBOURNE TRANSPORT DISPUTE
Melbourne's train services are expected to return to normal by early next week, following last night's temporary breakthrough in the Industrial Relations Commission.
The Public Transport Corporation agreed to reinstate train maintenance inspectors in return for the unions lifting all work bans.
The Commission will try to broker an agreement between the parties in the next seven days.
The Transport Minister Robin Cooper has welcomed the move, saying he expects full train services by early next week.
Trades Hall Council secretary Leigh Hubbard is also pleased, but he says the deal could have been struck earlier.
TAX RISE COULD FORCE ALCOHOL RETAILERS OUT OF BUSINESS
Carlton and United Breweries has warned that the 15 per cent rise in wholesale sales tax on alcohol could force some retailers out of business.
The brewer is warning State Governments must act quickly to establish systems to return the difference between the new, higher wholesale sales tax and the previous State-based fees.
Carlton and United spokesman Brendan McClements says the company has been speaking with every State Goverment in a bid to ensure no retailer is forced out of business.
"It's obviously a difficult area," he said.
"The negotiations have been useful, but we need to continue to work through the problem."
LIQUOR PRICES MAY RISE IN NEW SOUTH WALES
Liquor retailers in New South Wales say they may have to consider increasing prices immediately.
Their assessment follows the High Court ruling that the collection of tax on liquor, tobacco and petrol by the states is unconstitutional.
Liquor retailers are to be hit with an a 15 per cent tax by the Commonwealth to make up for lost state revenue following the high court ruling.

But the Liquor Retailers Association says retailers are being double taxed as they have already paid taxes in the form of licence fees to the State Government covering them up to the 15th of Janurary next year and totalling around $130 million.
The Association says the State Government has declared there will be no refund of the advance taxes and retailers will be left with no choice but to pass on the loss to consumers.
The Association is currently in talks with State Treasury officials but a spokesman says no progress is being made.
